nodes.bodyText:
Use case:

you have a triton kernel or custom operator
Inductor will make one of the following assumptions: "all inputs must have the same exact strides as the traced FX graph", "all inputs must have the same dense stride order as traced FX graph", "the operator/kernel is stride agnostic". For custom operators this is configurable at the creation of the operator, for triton kernels this is not currently configurable today
The assumption inductor makes might be different from what the user wanted, so ideally the user should be able to override the configuration.

I'm not sure what the API for this should look like. Options:
# Option 1: some config outside of the compiled region
torch._inductor.override_stride_constraints(op_or_kernel, "arg", REQUIRE_FIXED_STRIDES)

# Option 2: some annotation inside the compiled region:
custom_op(torch._inductor.stride_hint(x, "require_exact"), y)
annotation on a per-call level is probably better for debugging?
Thoughts? @eellison @FindHao @oulgen
cc @ezyang @chauhang @penguinwu @voznesenskym @EikanWang @jgong5 @Guobing-Chen @XiaobingSuper @zhuhaozhe @blzheng @wenzhe-nrv @jiayisunx @ipiszy @yf225 @chenyang78 @kadeng @muchulee8 @ColinPeppler @amjames @desertfire @oulgen @aakhundov

🐛 Describe the bug
We are planning upgrading our python environment from 3.8 to 3.10, because pytorch has deprecated python 3.8 recently.
But we found that there are performance gaps between python 3.8 and 3.10 when testing benchmarks/dynamo suites.
After debugging and try different configurations, we found that it might related to libiomp5.so and environment variable KMP_AFFINITY.
Performance



Python
Dev
name
batch_size
speedup
abs_latency
compilation_latency




3.8
Cpu
BERT_pytorch
2
1.83045
21.87665
28.22332


3.10
Cpu
BERT_pytorch
2
2.509247
403.2253
25.30055



Observations:

When LD_PRELOAD=libiomp5.so and KMP_AFFINITY are set, it shows performance regression. Unset one of them, performance is back to normal.

export LD_PRELOAD=${CONDA_PREFIX:-"$(dirname $(which conda))/../"}/lib/libiomp5.so
export KMP_AFFINITY=granularity=fine,compact,1,0

And we found that above configurations are set, there is only 1 core running on process pt_main_thread which might be the root cause of this poor performance on Python 3.10.



It can only be reproduce by executing all the model for each suite.py, which means that we cannot reproduce by executing only 1 model by passing --only BERT_pytorch

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
It would be pretty awesome if torch.compile would work with the zig C++ compiler which is invoked as zig c++ which uses llvm under the hood so should be (mostly?) fine compatibility-wise.
I want to deploy apps that use pytorch with torch.compile to systems that don't and won't have a c++ compiler available so I thought that it would be nice to bundle the app together with the zig toolchain to have a portable c++ compiler that can be used by torch.compile. Then I can just use the app with the env var CXX set to zig c++.
But that fails here
subprocess.check_output([cxx, "--version"])
where it is assumed that the CXX command doesn't contain spaces I think? That won't work with zig c++
Let me know what you think :) Hopefully I'm not alone with this kind of request.
Alternatives

I can just write a wrapper bash script around zig c++ and call it e.g. zig-c++
I could use https://github.com/rsms/llvmbox/ instead
I could use a conda env which can come with a C++ compiler AFAIU

Additional context
I think there would also be the need to adjust the _is_apple_clang function which assumes that the version string starts with Apple. Although I'm not sure about how this would have to be handled.

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
When a job hangs on a torch.cuda.synchronize(), it is rarely due to that particular torch.cuda.synchronize() call. Instead, something else in the CUDA queue that was already asynchronously queued that is causing the hang (typically a NCCL call or something). When this has happened, we will unpredictably hang at some later point in time, either when the next kernel put on the queue gets stuck because the queue is full, OR we block waiting for the entire queue to flush, which is what happens with torch.cuda.synchronize(). Because the synchronize() call is so likely to trigger the hang, it is the most likely thing to show up when you see hung jobs and then everyone concludes it's a PT2 problem when it's not.
Unfortunately, PT2 generates a lot of torch.cuda.synchronize() calls when it hasn't quiesced yet. Specifically, when we do autotuning, we end up doing a synchronize:
  File "/dev/shm/uid-99/dea1e454-seed-nspid4026560790_cgpid9965291-ns-4026560787/torch/_inductor/runtime/triton_heuristics.py", line 818, in run
    self.autotune_to_one_config(*args, grid=grid, **kwargs)
  File "/dev/shm/uid-99/dea1e454-seed-nspid4026560790_cgpid9965291-ns-4026560787/torch/_inductor/runtime/triton_heuristics.py", line 720, in autotune_to_one_config
    timings = self.benchmark_all_configs(*args, **kwargs)
  File "/dev/shm/uid-99/dea1e454-seed-nspid4026560790_cgpid9965291-ns-4026560787/torch/_dynamo/utils.py", line 272, in time_wrapper
    r = func(*args, **kwargs)
  File "/dev/shm/uid-99/dea1e454-seed-nspid4026560790_cgpid9965291-ns-4026560787/torch/_inductor/runtime/triton_heuristics.py", line 695, in benchmark_all_configs
    timings = {
  File "/dev/shm/uid-99/dea1e454-seed-nspid4026560790_cgpid9965291-ns-4026560787/torch/_inductor/runtime/triton_heuristics.py", line 696, in <dictcomp>
    launcher: self.bench(launcher, *args, **kwargs)
  File "/dev/shm/uid-99/dea1e454-seed-nspid4026560790_cgpid9965291-ns-4026560787/torch/_inductor/runtime/triton_heuristics.py", line 667, in bench
    return do_bench_gpu(kernel_call, rep=40, fast_flush=True)
  File "/dev/shm/uid-99/dea1e454-seed-nspid4026560790_cgpid9965291-ns-4026560787/torch/_inductor/runtime/runtime_utils.py", line 118, in do_bench_gpu
    return triton_do_bench(*args, **kwargs)[0]
  File "/dev/shm/uid-99/dea1e454-seed-nspid4026560790_cgpid9965291-ns-4026560787/triton/testing.py", line 104, in do_bench
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
  File "/dev/shm/uid-99/dea1e454-seed-nspid4026560790_cgpid9965291-ns-4026560787/torch/cuda/__init__.py", line 949, in synchronize

NB: this code was recently changed in #132827 but I think synchronize calls are still made.
It would be really great if we could figure out a way to not have to do a full CUDA synchronization. Remote autotuning service would be a sledgehammer way to solve the problem, but maybe there is something simpler we can do short term.

            metrics_end_time = datetime.now()  # Record metrics computation end time
            metrics_elapsed_time = (metrics_end_time - metrics_start_time).total_seconds()
            logger.debug(f"Batch {batch_idx} metrics computation completed in {metrics_elapsed_time:.2f} seconds.")

            all_metrics.append(pd.Series(sgs_metrics))

            end_time = datetime.now()  # Record end time
            elapsed_time = (end_time - start_time).total_seconds()
            logger.debug(f"Batch {batch_idx} processed in {elapsed_time:.2f} seconds.")

    avg_metrics = pd.DataFrame(all_metrics).mean()
    avg_sdr = avg_metrics['sdr']
    logger.info(f"Average SDR: {avg_sdr}")

    return avg_sdr

    """Export the FP32 PyTorch model to an ONNX model."""
    logger.info(f"Exporting model to ONNX with inputs of shape: {[x.shape for x in example_inputs]}")

        pt_fp32_model=model,
        save_path=save_path,
        example_inputs=example_inputs,
        opset_version=opset_version,
        verbose=True,
    )

    """Quantize the ONNX model using Intel Neural Compressor."""
    from neural_compressor.quantization import fit
    from neural_compressor.config import PostTrainingQuantConfig
    from neural_compressor.data import DataLoader

    tuning_criterion = TuningCriterion(max_trials=100)
    accuracy_criterion = AccuracyCriterion(higher_is_better=False, tolerable_loss=0.01)
    quantization_config = PostTrainingQuantConfig(
        approach="static",
        tuning_criterion=tuning_criterion,
        accuracy_criterion=accuracy_criterion,
        device="cpu",
        backend="onnxrt_qdq",
        op_type_dict = {
            "aten::linalg_solve": FP32,  # 尝试使用全称
            "linalg_solve": FP32,
            "linalg": FP32,  # 更泛化地覆盖 linalg 操作
            "Linear": FP32,
            "GroupNorm": FP32,
            "LayerNorm": FP32,
    }
    )

    q_model = fit(
        model=onnx_model_path,
        conf=quantization_config,
        calib_dataloader=calib_dataloader,
        eval_func=eval_func,
    )

    q_model.save(quantized_model_path)

        original_len = len(dataset)
        truncated_len =  int(original_len * percentage)

🐛 Describe the bug
In a recent PR - #132912 - we came across a nasty silent incorrectness bug. This prompted me to think about a few invariants that we should maintain

if var.mutable_local is MutableSideEffects - var.source must not be None
if var.mutable_local is MutableLocal - var.source must be None (this was in violation in the above issue, making side effects infra to do funky things)
if var.mutable_local is None - var must be a ConstantVariable (this could be relaxed and needs more thought, TupleVariable with constants etc) - This will ensure that we track mutable_local correctly in all cases.

We should probably change the attr name mutable_local to something else. The local in the name suggest to me that the tracked object is created inside the frame (as opposed to existing). Some suggestions for rename are
var.mutable_local to var.mutation_type (Not fully convinced that this good name, suggestions welcome)
MutableLocal to MutableNew (even local is confusing - is it from f_locals? Or is it created inside the frame?)
MutableSideEffects to MutableExisting (opposite of  MutableNew)

class M(torch.nn.Module):

with torch.no_grad():
    m=M()

    x=torch.tensor([2.])

    unflattened = torch.export.unflatten(exported)
    print(unflattened.graph)

    assert m(x)==200.0

    %linear_1 : [num_users=1] = call_function[target=torch.ops.aten.linear.default](args = (%linear, %weight), kwargs = {})
    return linear_1

linear is now not representing a torch.nn.Linear but something different - two calls to torch.ops.aten.linear. Its not a correctness issue in this case, but might be in other cases?
Anyways, the modules are not "properly preserved" as I see it. We had a module that is a linear layer, and that module was called twice, now we have a module that is two linear layers that is called once.

print(f"{module.training=}")  # True

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
I was adding reset_sharded_param to lazy_init but hit CI error #132954
pytest -s test/distributed/_composable/fsdp/test_fully_shard_comm.py -k test_unshard_async
I minimized repo below and it became a replicate/fully_shard question
we use DDP at root model, replicate(model.cuda()). Inside root model, we use FSDP2 for a submodule, fully_shard(model.linears). Before the forward, we have model.linears[0].weight in DTensor. Inside root forward but before model.linears[0].forward,  we have model.linears[0].weight in torch.Tensor (unsharded)
that's why it errors out by calling .unshard() -> lazy_init -> reset_sharded_param. reset_sharded_param assumes it's DTensor and access ._local_tensor but found there is no such attribute
class TestFullyShardUnshardMultiProcess(FSDPTest):
    @property
    def world_size(self) -> int:
        return min(torch.cuda.device_count(), 2)

    @skip_if_lt_x_gpu(2)
    def test_unshard_async(self):
        class ToyModel(nn.Module):
            def __init__(self, dim: int):
                super().__init__()
                self.linears = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(dim, dim, bias=False), nn.Linear(dim, dim, bias=False), nn.Linear(dim, dim, bias=False))
                self.proj = nn.Linear(dim, dim, bias=False)

            def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor):
                assert isinstance(self.linears[0].weight.data, DTensor), f"{type(self.linears[0].weight.data)=}"
                y = self.linears(x)
                y = self.proj(y)
                return y

        batch_size, dim = 2, 8
        torch.manual_seed(42)
        model = ToyModel(dim)
        fully_shard(model.linears[0])
        fully_shard(model.linears[1])
        fully_shard(model.linears[2])
        fully_shard(model.linears)
        replicate(model.cuda())
        torch.manual_seed(42 + self.rank + 1)
        inp = torch.randn((batch_size, dim), device="cuda")
        self.assertTrue(isinstance(model.linears[0].weight.data, DTensor))
        model(inp).sum()

🐛 Describe the bug
Environment

PyTorch 2.4.0
Kubernetes, launching distributed PyTorchJob (1 master and 1 worker replica) with KubeFlow Training Operator
Launching with torchrun
Using etcd-v2 as the rendezvous backend

Error
The training run fails immediately on startup with the error etcd.EtcdKeyNotFound: Key not found : /torch/elastic/store on the worker pod. The master pod errors out with torch.distributed.elastic.rendezvous.api.RendezvousClosedError. Subsequent restarts fail also due to the rendezvous being closed.
From the debug logs, it seems like when the master joins the rendezvous first it needs to wait for all participants so is stuck waiting here. When the worker joins, all participants are ready so it completes the _RendezvousJoinOp first and calls RendezvousStoreInfo.build here first. Because the worker reaches this method first, the master has not yet written the master address info to /torch/elastic/store here yet, so the worker's call to retrieve this info here fails and the worker closes the rendezvous.
Reversing this order by adding a brief sleep to the master pod (so the worker is the one waiting and the master completes the rendezvous first) seems to resolve this issue. Adding a sleep right before the store.get call if rank != 0 so that the master has time to write the keys also seems to work. I assume adding retry logic to the store.get call should also work.

nodes.bodyText:
One piece of compiled autograd debugging that I think might aid in debugging would be that:

in the "non-compiled autograd flow", when you inspect a given backward graph and I see some input that is not named tangents*, I know that it is a saved activation
I can inspect the corresponding forward graph to see exactly how it was computed, and what user code it was computed from (through the stack trace info)
This info is lost in the compiled autograd graph: in the compiled autograd graph, you see a big list of inputs, but you do not know where they came from.

One thing that might be nice would be something like: when compiled autograd pulls a bunch of saved activations from a given node on the autograd tape, it checks to see if that node is a CompiledBackwardNode. If it is, also log for that particular input:
(1) the aot_id of this backward node (so you can correlate it with the forward - we can store the aot_id directly on the node: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/torch/_functorch/_aot_autograd/runtime_wrappers.py#L1477)
(2) the index of this particular activation from that backward node (so we can map it to, e.g. "output 7 of forward graph 5")
example code:
import torch

@torch.compile
def f(x):
    tmp1 = x.sin()
    print("graph break!")
    return tmp1.sin()

x = torch.randn(4, requires_grad=True)
out = f(x)
with torch._dynamo.compiled_autograd.enable(torch.compile):
    out.sum().backward()

If I run the above with TORCH_LOGS="compiled_autograd,aot", I get the below graphs. I happen to know that in the compiled autograd graph, inputs[1] and inputs[2] correspond to the saved activation in forward graphs 1 and 2 (primals_1, mul nodes), but it would be nice to be able to tell that strictly from the logs.

It looks like this code is not enabled for SM90 systems but I don't see any reason for that.
import torch
from torch.sparse import to_sparse_semi_structured

def run_sparse_matmul(M, N, K, force_cutlass=False, dtype=torch.float16, device='cuda'):
    torch.sparse.SparseSemiStructuredTensor._FORCE_CUTLASS = force_cutlass

    # Create sparse semi-structured matrix
    x = torch.randn(M, N, dtype=dtype, device=device)
    dense_weights = torch.randn(K, N, dtype=dtype, device=device)
    sparse_weights = to_sparse_semi_structured(dense_weights)

    torch.nn.functional.linear(x, sparse_weights)

# Fails with:
# sparse_semi_structured_mad_op : Supported only on GPUs with compute capability 8.x
run_sparse_matmul(64, 64, 64, True)

# Fails with:
# CUDA error: architecture mismatch when calling `cusparseLtInit(&handle)`
run_sparse_matmul(64, 64, 64, False)

🐛 Describe the bug
Getting segmentation fault when using backward on  torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention's output.  Inputs are in torch.bfloat16.
code to reproduce the error:
import torch

query = (
        torch.empty(size=[2, 2, 49, 32], dtype=torch.bfloat16, device="cpu")
        .uniform_(-1, 1)
        .requires_grad_(True)
    )
key = (
        torch.empty(size=[2, 2, 49, 32], dtype=torch.bfloat16, device="cpu")
        .uniform_(-1, 1)
        .requires_grad_(True)
    )
value = (
        torch.empty(size=[2, 2, 49, 32], dtype=torch.bfloat16, device="cpu")
        .uniform_(-1, 1)
        .requires_grad_(True)
    )
breakpoint()
with torch.cpu.amp.autocast(enabled=True, dtype=torch.bfloat16):
    res = torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention(query, key, value, None, 0.0, False)

res_grad = torch.empty_like(res, device="cpu").uniform_(-1, 1)

res.backward(res_grad, retain_graph=True)

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
When using torch.library.opcheck(...) to test an operator, the test_aot_dispatch_dynamic step invokes the backward pass of the operator by passing gradient tensors whose strides are all zeros.
This is because these gradients are obtained by the backward of the .sum() operator, as seen here: 
  
    
      pytorch/torch/testing/_internal/optests/aot_autograd.py
    
    
         Line 108
      in
      32f9a80
    
  
  
    

        
          
           sm += i.sum().abs() 
        
    
  

 If I multiply i by 2 before calling .sum() the issue disappears.
I believe this can be considered an issue because tensors with strides of zero are uncommon in real workloads, thus not all operators might be ready to handle them. Forcing such a test on all operators might be too much to ask.
Versions
PyTorch nightly 2.5.0.dev20240718 py3.10_cuda12.1_cudnn9.1.0_0 installed via conda.
cc @anjali411 @zou3519

I am trying to apply torch.compile into vLLM, and I have met an issue that recompilation happens for each next token run. Thanks for the help from @anijain2305, I have narrow down the dynamo guard failure as

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Currently inplacing logic only extends to Pointwise uses. We should extend this to reductions.
For example, matmul_output of  LayerNorm can be inplaced below:
import torch
torch.set_default_device("cuda")
torch.set_grad_enabled(False)

batch_size = 32
seq_length = 50
hidden_size = 768

inp = torch.randn(batch_size, seq_length, hidden_size)
weight = torch.randn(hidden_size, hidden_size)

layer_norm = torch.nn.LayerNorm(hidden_size)

@torch.compile()
def foo(inp, weight):
    matmul_output = inp @ weight
    final_output = layer_norm(matmul_output)
    return final_output

foo(inp, weight)

This can help with both perf and memory.

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
Calling torch.lobpcg with a torch.cfloat (or equivalent complex values) raise RuntimeError: "lt_cpu" not implemented for 'ComplexFloat'
when comparing the euclidian norm of covergence criteria equation 9 from https://arxiv.org/pdf/1704.07458 at line 792 from the code converged = rerr < tol
Since rerr is a complex type the comparision to a pure float is rightfully not implemented.
Versions
torch==2.4.0
cc @albanD
nodes.title: lobpcg doesn't support complex

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
I am developing a pytorch extension for xpu. I am using pytorch upstream, not ipex. My extension needs to get the sycl::queue for a tensor. There doesn't seem to be a way to do this if you pip install torch. See https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/how-to-get-the-queue-for-xpu-device/207604 for some background.
Alternatives
No response
Additional context
